t: Design an Ordered Stream: One Array, One Forward Pointer
o: Pairs arrive with unique ids in 1..n but in arbitrary order; after each insert we must return the maximal run of consecutive values starting from the smallest id not yet returned. The example shows the mechanics: inserting id 3 first returns an empty list, then id 1 emits aaaaa because id 2 is still a hole, so inserting id 2 immediately flushes bbbbb and ccccc together; ids 5 and then 4 repeat the same pattern at the tail. Constraints are tiny (n <= 1000, exactly n inserts, unique ids), which means every slot is eventually written exactly once — a flat array indexed by id plus a pointer to the next expected id captures the whole state. Total pointer movement across all calls is at most n, so the amortized cost per insert is constant plus whatever chunk is emitted.
k: Store each value at data[id] and keep ptr = smallest id not yet returned; the chunk is data[ptr .. next hole).
The pointer never moves backward, so flushing costs O(n) total even though one insert may emit a long run.
An insert whose id differs from ptr can emit nothing — a single gap blocks all output until it is filled.

a.n: Approach 1: Direct-Address Array with Moving Pointer
a.i: Allocate n+1 slots (index 0 unused so ids align) and remember the leftmost unfilled id. Each insert writes its slot, then walks the pointer forward while slots are filled and slices out the contiguous chunk. Because each of the n slots causes at most one pointer advance over the stream lifetime, the design is asymptotically optimal and trivially correct.
s: Allocate data of size n+1; set ptr = 1.
insert(idKey, value): write data[idKey] = value; if idKey != ptr, return an empty list.
Remember start = ptr; advance ptr while data[ptr] is filled and within bounds.
Return data[start:ptr] — empty when the pointer did not move.
a.t: O(1) amortized per insert plus O(chunk) to build each returned slice; O(n) overall since every slot advances the pointer at most once.
a.sp: O(n) — one array slot per possible id.

a.n: Approach 2: Hash Map of Pending Pairs
a.i: Keep only arrived pairs in a hash map and delete entries as they are flushed. Behavior is identical, but memory tracks the number of out-of-order holes rather than the whole id range, it needs no upfront allocation sized to n, and membership checks replace null/empty sentinels. For these dense constraints the array wins on constants; for sparse or huge id ranges the map is the right structure.
s: Maintain a map id -> value and ptr = 1.
On insert, store the pair; if idKey != ptr, return an empty list.
While the map contains ptr, append map[ptr] to the chunk, delete it, and increment ptr.
a.t: O(n) total — every pair is written once and flushed once, with O(1) average map operations.
a.sp: O(h) where h is the number of currently held out-of-order pairs — worst case O(n).

w: In an interview, ship Approach 1 first and lead with the invariant: ptr always equals the smallest unreleased id, so correctness reduces to never emitting past a hole. Pitfalls: off-by-one errors from 1-based ids landing in 0-based arrays (allocate n+1); stopping the flush at n instead of at the first gap; rebuilding sorted output by sorting on every insert, which is pointless given direct addressing. In C++ the empty-string sentinel works only because values have length 5 — call that out or carry a parallel boolean array. Follow-ups: support duplicate ids (reject or overwrite policy), unknown n (the hash-map variant), or expose the output as a lazy iterator instead of a materialized list.
